newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia poll delay "disappoints" U.S.'s Cohen.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia poll delay "disappoints" U.S.'s Cohen.

text.p: The U.S. defence secretary on Thursday sharply criticised a new delay in Bosnian municipal elections, calling it another failure by outside civilian agencies helping to rejuvenate the war-shattered country.
"I can only say it is disappointing. It will complicate matters," William Cohen said, adding this would not delay the final departure of U.S. forces from Bosnia in mid-1998.

Cohen said the delay by the Organisation on Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) was simply another sign that civilian agencies were not doing their part to end the requirement for military peacekeeping in Bosnia.

"I am disappointed with those who are responsible for setting up and acquiring the (election) monitors, the financial resources in order to allow the elections to go forward," he told a news conference. "But it will not in my judgment deter us from carrying out the (military) mission until its completion in June of 1998."
He spoke after the OSCE announced a second delay in municipal elections, which had been scheduled for July, until September 13-14.

Cohen had lunch with U.S. troops at camp Dobol near the tense northern Bosnian town of Brcko and was briefed by U.S. General George Joulwan, who commands all NATO forces in Europe, and senior U.S. officers in Bosnia.
He had his picture taken with U.S. and Russian members of the NATO-led peacekeeping Bosnia force of 31,000 and said he was proud of the job they had done.
But he said a final peace was up to the former warring factions and Serbs, Moslems and Croats must have a "change of heart" and realise that peacekeeping forces would not remain after mid-1998.
"What they really need to do is stop hoping in some way that this decision is going to be delayed, that we are going to stay. That is not going to happen, " he said.

Cohen, who replaced William Perry in January, is nearing the end of a trip to Germany, Bosnia, Italy and Belgium. He stressed repeatedly that U.S. troops in the NATO-led force would leave Bosnia on schedule and not return even if war broke out again.

Germany and Britain said that other peacekeeping troops would also leave, although some European officials have predicted that another military force, perhaps sponsored by the Western European Union, could then be sent into Bosnia.

Cohen arrived at nearby Tuzla on a C-17 U.S. military cargo plane from Aviano, Italy, at midday on a warm and sunny day. "I was planning on snow and mud and a lot of rain. But you pulled out the sun for me," he said.
He later flew to Rome for dinner and talks with Italian Defence Minister Beniamino Andreatta.

Cohen, a defence policy veteran who served 24 years in Congress, said when taking office that the United States could not afford to be the world's chief policeman and peacekeeper while coping with a shrinking military budget and costly modernisation of its cold-war weaponry.

At Camp McGovern he said civilian authorities had failed to speedily carry out promises to rejuvenate Bosnia's financial and civic infrastructure. He noted that only half of the rebuilding funds provided for Bosnia in the past year had been assigned to specific projects.
Cohen will go to Brussels on Friday for a day of meetings with NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana and permanent representatives to the alliance before reutrning to Washington .
